youtube_title: X-Men Toys Were Ruled 'Not Human' — to Cut Import Duty
caption: In Toy Biz v. United States (2003), the trade court held X-Men figures weren't 'dolls representing only human beings' because of non-human features — putting them in a lower-duty toy category under the tariff schedule of the time.
script: Marvel's own toy company stood in court and swore the X-Men aren't human. To pay less tax. [disclaimer] Meet Toy Biz. Toy Biz makes Marvel action figures. Wolverine, Storm, the whole team. The toys are made overseas. So they come in through customs. And customs has to pick a category. Back then, a doll that shows a human being pays twelve percent at the border. A toy that shows an animal or a creature pays less. About seven percent. Customs looks at the X-Men and says, these are people. Dolls. Pay the big tax. Toy Biz goes to the trade court and argues the opposite. Look closer. They're mutants. Wolverine has claws. Others have fangs and tentacles. Wait. A superhero company is arguing its own heroes aren't human? You see, the court asked one question. Does this toy show a human being? Even one feature that isn't human can be enough to say no. It's like a cat in a suit. Still a cat. In two thousand three, the court agrees. These figures are not dolls. Cheaper tax. Not every figure won. One still counted as a doll. And by the time of the ruling, those toy taxes were already gone for new imports. So the company that sells the X-Men as heroes proved in court they're creatures. [loop] So the next time someone calls your action figure a doll, remember
